title.en: Sizes and distances rarely share one scale

summary: Use separate declared scale factors for body sizes and separations when one scale would make the scene unusable.
objective: Keep astronomical scenes legible without implying that their proportions are true.
applies_when: Planets, moons, stars or atoms are shown together with their separations.
Orbits or distances are drawn at a size that fits a screen.
The viewer might infer relative sizes or distances from the image.
example_prompts: Show the inner planets with their orbits and be clear about the scale.
Build a scale model I can switch between size scale and distance scale.
negative_signals: Single-body scenes where no separation is shown.
True-scale models where both can honestly share one factor.
not_for: Single-body scenes where no separation is shown.
True-scale models where both can honestly share one factor.

principles: Astronomical size and separation differ by orders of magnitude, so a single-scale model is usually impractical: making both accurate at once requires a model that spreads over a great distance, which is why educational activities note that displaying both accurately is difficult or impossible in a small model.
Using two scale factors is legitimate and standard. Failing to say so is what turns a useful diagram into a misconception, because viewers routinely take planet spacing from illustrations.

The choice should follow the question: a scene about seasons or phases needs correct geometry and can compress distance, while a scene about the emptiness of space needs correct distance and can drop body detail.
The same problem appears at molecular and structural scales whenever object size and separation differ by orders of magnitude.
implementation: Keep true values in the model and apply separate declared factors for body radius and for separation.
Display both factors persistently, and include them in exports.

Offer a switch to a single-scale mode where the emptiness itself is part of the explanation. It is a useful option, not an obligation: a scene answering a question about geometry or phase can disclose its factors without carrying a second view.
Use a familiar reference object or a scale bar so the compression is perceptible.

Uniformly scaling center separations preserves center-to-center directions. That can preserve the spherical distant-observer phase model, but independent radius scaling changes apparent sizes, parallax, finite-observer sightlines and shadow cones. Compute these from true geometry, preserve the relevant ratios, or label the depiction illustrative; disclosure alone does not correct a mis-scaled calculation.
observable_checks: If single-scale mode is offered, confirm that it uses one declared factor for body sizes and separations and preserves their true relative proportions.
Compare the ratio of two drawn separations against the true ratio; a scene that also compresses non-uniformly should say so.
Confirm the scale factors appear in the scene and in any exported image.

Check the particular preserved quantity: center directions under uniform separation scaling, and phase only under the declared spherical distant-observer construction. Verify finite-observer appearance, apparent size, parallax and shadows against true geometry when claimed as accurate.

creative_affordances: Beautiful compressed solar-system scenes are the norm and remain valid with disclosure.
Logarithmic or segmented distance scales are legitimate alternatives when labelled.
known_limits: Authored scale guidance citing an educational statement about the difficulty of single-scale models; it asserts no specific astronomical distance or radius.
It does not prescribe scale factors for any particular scene.

claims.statement: Because planetary sizes and orbital distances differ by orders of magnitude, it is difficult or even impossible to display both planet size and distance accurately in a small model, and a model accurate in both would need to extend over a very large distance.
claims.scope: Practical scale-model limitations for the solar system; it does not provide specific sizes or distances.
